questions.question: For equal-mean integrable losses, an analyst selects t 0 and checks $F_Y(t)\ge F_X(t)$ at one t<t 0 and $F_Y(t)\le F_X(t)$ at one t>=t 0. Does this establish direct thicker-tailed comparison?
options: No; each inequality must hold over its entire threshold interval.
Yes; one threshold on each side is the complete criterion.
Yes; equal means automatically fill in all unobserved CDF values.
No; each observed inequality must be strict instead.

questions.question: Y is directly thicker-tailed than X with the same finite mean. Why does this describe dispersion rather than a uniformly larger loss?
options: The Y CDF must be smaller than X’s at every threshold.
The Y CDF must be larger than X’s at every threshold.
The Y law must be a deterministic increase of every X outcome.
The Y CDF comparison reverses between lower and upper sides.

questions.question: A bounded loss Y on[0,2] is directly thicker-tailed than a certain loss X=1. What does the word thicker mean in this comparison?
options: A requirement that Y have unbounded support.
A relative two-sided CDF dispersion comparison at fixed mean.
A requirement that Y have an infinite mean.
A requirement that Y’s tail decay as an inverse power.

questions.question: For equal-mean integrable losses, the known direct thicker-tailed comparisons give arrows X to Z and Y to Z, each toward the thicker law. Do these two arrows establish that Y is indirectly thicker-tailed than X?
options: Yes; paths to a common endpoint give the required comparison direction.
Yes; the common mean alone identifies the endpoint loss distributions.
No; these arrows do not supply a directed chain from X to Y.
Yes; any direct comparison can be reversed before composing the arrows.

questions.question: X and Y have exactly the same integrable loss law. Do they meet the weak direct thicker-tailed criterion in both directions?
options: No; direct comparison requires a strictly positive tail difference.
No; their means must differ for any comparison.
Yes; but only when the common loss is constant.
Yes; both CDF inequalities are equalities at every threshold.

questions.question: X is certainly 1 and Y is 0 or 2 equally likely. At the proposed crossing t 0=1, what CDF values and endpoint convention make the direct comparison valid?
options: F_Y(1)=1/2<F_X(1)=1; the point belongs to the upper interval.
F_Y(1)=F_X(1)=1/2; equality is required at every discrete crossing.
F_Y(1)=1>F_X(1)=1/2; the point belongs to the lower interval.
F_Y(1)=0<F_X(1)=1; the Y mass at 0 is excluded from its CDF.

questions.question: X is certainly 1 and Y is 0 or 3 equally likely. Its CDF is above X’s below 1 and below X’s from 1 to 3. Does Y nevertheless fail the direct thicker-tailed definition?
options: No; one correctly directed CDF crossing suffices without a mean condition.
No; their shared non-negative support guarantees equal means.
Yes; its mean 1.5 differs from X’s mean 1.
Yes; the upper support of Y exceeds the upper support of X.

questions.question: Above a valid crossing threshold, F_X(t)=0.9 and F_Y(t)=0.8. What strict tail probabilities express the thicker upper side of Y?
Non-negative losses have F_X(0)=0.1 and F_Y(0)=0.3, on the lower side of their crossing. What do those values say specifically about zero-loss probabilities?
options: Y has zero-loss probability 0.7, compared with X’s 0.9.
Both have zero-loss probability zero because a CDF cannot include atoms.
The two zero-loss probabilities must agree because the means agree.
Y has zero-loss probability 0.3, compared with X’s 0.1.

questions.question: A two-point loss on{0,8} must have mean 2. What probability is required at 8 to preserve that mean when comparing dispersion?
Two distinct integrable loss laws have equal finite mean, and Y is directly thicker-tailed than X. Can they be comparable in either direction of stochastic order?
options: Yes; X is smaller in stochastic order because the upper-side tail comparison suffices.
Yes; Y is smaller in stochastic order because the lower-side CDF comparison suffices.
No; either global stochastic direction with equal finite means would force identical laws.
Yes; both stochastic directions hold because the two finite loss means are equal.

questions.question: Two continuous CDFs meet the direct lower/upper sign conditions at t 0. Why must their CDF difference equal zero at t 0, unlike a discrete jump?
options: Continuity makes the lower and upper side limits meet.
Equal means force the CDFs equal at every threshold.
The upper-side condition is strict at t 0 by definition.
A continuous CDF cannot have a lower-side positive difference.

questions.question: X has masses 1/2,1/4,1/4 at 1,2,3; Y has masses 1/4,1/4,1/2 at 0,1,3. Both means are 1.75. Their CDF difference F_Y-F_X is positive on[0,1),zero on[1,2),negative on[2,3). Which crossing thresholds work?
options: Only t 0=1.
Every t 0 in[1,2].
Only t 0=2.
Every t 0 in[0,3].

questions.question: X is certainly 1 and Y is 0 or 2 equally likely. Apply the same map z->3+2 z to both. Which certain-reference value, dispersed outcomes and crossing follow?
options: Reference 2; dispersed 0 or 4 equally likely; crossing 2.
Reference 5; dispersed 3 or 4 equally likely; crossing 5.
Reference 3; dispersed 5 or 7 equally likely; crossing 3.
Reference 5; dispersed 3 or 7 equally likely; crossing 5.

questions.question: X is certainly 1 and Y is 0 or 3 with probabilities 2/3,1/3, so both have mean 1. Reflect both by z->3-z on[0,3]. Which comparison holds for the reflected laws?
options: The reflected Y is directly thicker-tailed than the reflected constant X=2.
The reflected X is directly thicker-tailed than the reflected Y.
The reflected means differ, preventing direct comparison.
The reflected laws coincide because reflection removes dispersion.

questions.question: X is certainly 1 and Y is 0 or 2 equally likely. Squaring is increasing on their non-negative domain. Do X squared and Y squared retain the direct equal-mean thicker-tailed comparison?
options: Yes; every increasing map preserves this dispersion relation.
Yes; their transformed means remain 1 and 1.
No; their transformed means are 1 and 2.
No; the transformed means agree but the CDF orientation is reversed.

questions.question: Integrable X,Y have equal mean and Y is directly thicker-tailed at t 0. A loss Z is specified by the valid CDF $F_Z=(1-\theta)F_X+\theta F_Y$ with $0<\theta<1$, and has the same mean. Why does Z remain directly thicker-tailed than X?
options: The positive coefficient makes the upper-side difference positive.
$F_Z-F_X=\theta(F_Y-F_X)$ preserves both signs at t 0.
The new CDF must coincide with F_Y at every threshold.
The crossing must move by the additive amount theta.

questions.question: Integrable equal-mean laws each satisfy the direct thicker-tailed criterion relative to the other, possibly using different crossing thresholds. Can their laws be distinct?
options: Yes; opposite direct comparisons freely allow distinct laws with the same mean.
No; every direct comparison requires a unique threshold shared by both laws.
No; the two sign patterns leave a global CDF direction, and equal finite means force equality.
Yes; direct comparison ignores all thresholds between the two splits.

questions.question: X is 1 or 3 equally likely; Y is 0,2,4 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4. Both means are 2. The CDF difference F_Y-F_X has signs+,-,+,- on successive intervals[0,1),[1,2),[2,3),[3,4). What direct conclusion follows?
options: Y is directly thicker-tailed because it has wider support.
X is directly thicker-tailed because its CDF reaches one sooner.
Y is directly thicker-tailed because equal means remove extra sign changes.
Neither law is directly thicker-tailed than the other.

questions.question: On support 0,1,2,3,4, three loss laws have probability numerators A=(0,2,8,2,0),B=(0,2,9,0,1),C=(1,0,10,0,1), all divided by 12. Each mean is 2. B is directly thicker than A with split 3; C is directly thicker than B with split 1. What follows for C relative to A?
options: C is indirectly thicker, but its alternating CDF signs prevent direct comparison.
C is directly thicker because direct comparisons are transitive.
C is neither directly nor indirectly thicker because the endpoint CDFs cross repeatedly.
A is directly thicker than C because the chain reverses dispersion.
